Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 74
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Editor
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Being Criticised: Being criticised or corrected, Violence: Violence, Offender Cues: Seeing the offender
  Maladaptive Strategies: Distraction: I distract myself with something else, Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me, Avoid Feelings: Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
  Negative Appraisals: Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Vignette:
Liam had always been a meticulous editor, priding himself on the precision and clarity of his work. At seventy-four, he found solace in the rhythm of sentences and the structure of paragraphs. But in the quiet moments, when the world outside his office faded into silence, memories of a different kind would seep in, uninvited. He was caught in a battle between his profession and his past, a past that had left him tethered to anger and fear, a past that haunted him like a shadow.

It had been years since the incident that changed everything. He could still recall the specifics with startling clarity—the way the light filtered through the curtains in their small apartment, casting a golden hue over the chaos of their lives. It was during one of their heated arguments, the kind that would escalate beyond words into something far more menacing. As she had raised her hand, the world around him had shrunk to that singular moment. The memory struck him like a snapshot, vivid yet disjointed, each fragment feeling as if it belonged to someone else. He could see the anger etched on her face, hear the sharpness of her voice, and feel the overwhelming rush of panic that had consumed him. It was as if he had become an object in her grip, dehumanized, stripped of his agency.

The years had passed since that fateful day, but the scars remained fresh. Liam had developed a keen sensitivity to criticism, even the most benign kind, which could send him spiraling back to that moment of violence. He would feel a wave of nausea wash over him when a colleague suggested a change in his editing style or when a friend pointed out a minor mistake in his work. Each instance felt like an echo of the past, a reminder of vulnerability that he could hardly bear. In those moments, he would often retreat into himself, distracting himself with trivial tasks, flipping through pages of manuscripts and editing as a means to escape the emotions threatening to surface. He had come to believe that allowing himself to feel any strong emotion would only lead him back to that place of rage, a place he had fought valiantly to avoid.

His avoidance extended beyond the emotional realm. Even the mention of her name, or anything that reminded him of her, would send him into a frenzied state of panic. He had meticulously crafted his life to exclude all traces of her presence. He stopped attending social events where he might encounter mutual friends who could stir up the past. His once vibrant social life had dwindled to a mere whisper of what it used to be, leaving him both isolated and relieved. Friendships faded, and laughter became a distant memory, replaced by the heavy silence of his apartment.

Yet it was the anger that lingered the longest. Liam found that whenever the memories resurfaced, they were accompanied by a fierce rage that felt both alien and consuming. He could recall the moments so vividly, each one a jarring image that left him breathless. “If only I had been stronger,” he would think, grappling with the notion that the abuse he suffered was a reflection of his character, a belief that had woven itself into the fabric of his identity. He often felt that the event had happened because of the sort of person he was, a deep-seated belief in his own inadequacies that only deepened his sense of despair.

It was during one particularly quiet evening, as he sat surrounded by stacks of manuscripts, that the weight of his experience became unbearable. The isolation, the anger, the ever-present fear—it all culminated in a moment of clarity. He realized he could no longer navigate this labyrinth of pain alone. After years of avoidance, he made the decision to seek help, driven by a flicker of hope that perhaps he could reclaim the emotions he had lost and understand the memories that felt so foreign.

As he sat in the waiting room of the therapist’s office, his heart raced with anxiety. What frightened him most was the thought of confronting the memories that had haunted him for so long. Yet, in the depths of that fear, there was also a glimmer of hope—hope that he might find a way to weave the fragments of his past into a narrative that no longer defined him, a narrative that would allow him to feel whole again.
